problem: The motoring curve is defined as "the pressure with fuel but no ignition". Standard usage is the pressure trace recorded while the engine is turned over without combustion; the presence of fuel is not part of the definition, and a student may think fuel must always be in the charge when the motoring curve is taken.
fix: The motoring curve is the cylinder pressure trace recorded when the engine is motored without combustion (no firing). It is the reference line on the p–θ plot; where the firing trace departs from it marks the end of ignition lag.

where: Section 2 and Exam traps, last bullet
problem: Section 2 puts peak pressure at 10°–15° aTDC but the end of the main flame sweep at 40°–45° aTDC, while the trap says "peak pressure belongs to the end of flame propagation". The two statements pull against each other and a student can conclude that pressure peaks at 42° aTDC.
fix: Say that peak pressure arrives near the end of the rapid burning phase, typically 10°–15° aTDC, while the flame is finishing the last pockets of charge; the burning that continues to about 40°–45° aTDC no longer raises pressure, and afterburning is the slow oxidation tail after that. Rewrite the trap as: peak pressure belongs to the end of the rapid burning (main) phase, not to afterburning.

problem: The symbol θ is first defined as crank position measured from TDC (negative before TDC), then reused in θ = 6 N t as a crank-angle interval. The same symbol for a position and a duration is confusing.
fix: Keep θ for crank position and write the conversion as Δθ = 6 N t = 0.006 N t_ms, with Δθ the crank-angle interval in degrees, N the speed in rev/min, t the time in seconds and t_ms the same time in milliseconds.

problem: "A reaction zone perhaps a millimetre thick" states only the upper end. Flame-front thickness in SI engines is usually quoted as a fraction of a millimetre up to about a millimetre.
fix: A thin flame front, a reaction zone typically a fraction of a millimetre to about a millimetre thick, moves into the unburnt mixture.
